S.01 — One night, four moments

One system, from the QR code on the table to the last number of the night.

19:40 — Table 12 seated

The guest scans.

No app, no download, no waiting for a menu. The QR code on the table opens your own menu — in English, Spanish or Arabic, chosen by the guest, not by you.

20:05 — Order placed

The order goes in.

Prices, VAT and the running total are computed in one place, so the number the guest sees is the number the till charges. No arithmetic at the table.

The kitchen gets the order.

One second later the ticket is in the kitchen, in the form a kitchen already reads. Nobody retypes anything, so nobody mistypes anything.

The owner closes.

Covers, revenue and what actually sold — the night, in the numbers you already use to run it. Not a report you have to build.

S.01 — What it replaces

A delivery app rents you
your own customers.

Then it charges a quarter of every order to keep renting them to you, and it keeps the record of who they are. Archon is the other arrangement.

Their marketplace

  • 25–30% taken on every order, forever
  • Their brand above yours, next to your competitors
  • They hold the guest's details, not you
  • Your price has to absorb their cut

Your system

  • No commission, just a flat fee, whatever the night does
  • Your own domain, your own room, nobody else's
  • Your guests and your orders sit in your database
  • The price on the menu is the price you keep

S.02 — How it starts

A QR code on the table. That is the whole install.

No app to download, no account to create. The guest points a camera at a QR code and your menu is open, the same menu the kitchen is cooking from, priced the way the till will charge.

For a table in a hurry, that is the difference between waiting for a busy waiter and knowing your food is being prepared.

S.03 — The order

Different teams. One ticket. No disagreement.

A restaurant is not one screen. The floor, the kitchen, the bar, the till and the office each need a different view of the same night — and they must never disagree about it.

Waiter

Opens a table, takes the order, delivers the dishes, closes the bill.

Kitchen

Tickets arrive in the order they were sent, with requirements spelt out.

Cashier

The bill adds up on its own, because nobody re-entered it.

Owner

Complete oversight: the money, the staff and which dishes actually paid for themselves.

S.04 — The site we build you

It should look like your restaurant. Not like software.

We build your landing page too — the real thing, with proper UI/UX, your menu, your logo, your photography and your words if you want, on your own domain. Not a template with your logo dropped into it.

The menu the guest opens is part of that same site, so scanning the QR code never throws them out of your space into someone else's app.

This page you are reading was built by the same hands.

S.05 — The owner's side

Eleven screens to run your business. The guest never sees them.

Behind the menu is the part you run the business from: what is on the menu, what sold, what is left, what to buy tomorrow, who worked, and how much came in. One private address, one PIN — total visibility and control.

S.10 — Questions

Asked before, answered plainly.

What does it cost?

A flat monthly fee, never a percentage of your orders — a busy Saturday costs exactly what a quiet Tuesday costs. We do not publish the number because it depends on the size of the room and how much menu there is to build. Fill in the set-up and we come back the same day with a figure; a fee quoted blind is one that somebody ends up regretting.

Do we have to replace our POS or our payment provider?

No. Archon covers the room: the menu, the ordering, the kitchen and the night's numbers. Card processing and delivery logistics stay with whoever handles them for you today, and we take no cut of either.

What happens to the data if we leave?

It is yours and it leaves with you. Menu, orders, guests and revenue are exportable at any time, without asking us and without a fee. A system that holds your data hostage is not a system; it is a lock and chain.

Our menu changes every week. Who edits it?

You do, online. Prices, dishes and availability live on the dashboard, so anyone on your team who has access can change the menu — no new software, no ticket filed with us because something ran out at 21:00. The self-service editor is inside the dashboard.

Is the Arabic real, or machine translated?

The layout is real: right-to-left is built into the system, not flipped with a stylesheet. The words are yours — we set up the fields and a native speaker on your side signs off the menu copy. We do not publish Arabic nobody has read.

Who owns the domain and the site?

You do. The site lives on your own domain, registered in the venue's name — not on a subdomain of ours. If we ever part ways, the address your guests already know keeps working and stays yours.

What happens on a Friday night when everything is full?

The guest's menu and ordering run in the browser against a database built for concurrent tables, not on a tablet in the corner that somebody has to keep awake. The part that fails under pressure in most venues is the retyping between the floor and the kitchen, and that step does not exist here.

How long from the menu to opening?

Days, not months, for a single venue with a menu that already exists. The step that takes real time is the service we stand through with your floor, and that one should not be rushed.

Archon — Set-up

Tell us the restaurant. We build it.

Everything below is what it takes to stand your system up — the address on the ticket, the VAT on the bill, the languages on the menu. It saves as you type, so you can leave and come back on the same device.

The venue

The name that goes on the site, on the dashboard and on every printed ticket.

Exactly as guests know it.

The short form you use on the sign or the logo. Leave empty to use the full name.

A short phrase. It becomes the description search engines read.

Where to find you

This lands on the site, in the map, and on the printed receipt. Get it exact — a wrong address on a ticket is a real problem, not a typo.

This sets your currency, your tax rate and your time zone further down. You can change any of them.

Open your restaurant in Google Maps, press Share, and paste the link. It sets the map on your site.

How you operate

The number of tables matters more than it looks: a table numbered above it is silently rejected when a guest scans, so count every table you will ever put a QR code on. Adding a few spare now costs nothing.

Opens, then closes. Past midnight is fine — 01:00 means one in the morning.

Leave as is if you keep the same hours all week.

If you never close, leave it blank.

Count the terrace and any table you might add this year. Too high costs nothing; too low breaks scanning.

Every "today" in your reports is computed from this.

Money

The tax rate is written into two places at once — what the guest sees and what the till charges. If it is wrong here, it is wrong on both, so it is worth checking with whoever does your books.

Set from your country. Write 0% if the venue is not registered.

Printed on the receipt. Legally required once registered.

As on the trade licence, if it differs from the name guests use.

Language and look

Pick every language a guest might want. Arabic is laid out right to left properly, not flipped with a stylesheet — but the words are yours, and we ask a native speaker on your side to sign them off before anything goes live.

Tap to add or remove. English is on by default — switch it off if your guests do not need it.

If you do not know them, leave these and send the logo below — we take the colours from it and show you before building.

SVG, PDF or the highest-resolution image you have. Up to 25 MB.

The room, the kitchen, three or four dishes. JPG, PNG or HEIC, the largest you have. Up to eight files.

This is what your site will be made of. Send nothing and we will find good photographs of your kind of cooking — the site will look right, but it will not be your room and it will not be your plates. Photographs off a phone, taken near a window, beat anything we can find for you.

A name is enough. If you have licence files, mention it and we will ask separately.

The menu

This is the one that takes us the longest and you the least. Send it however it exists — a PDF is best, and we read it almost perfectly. Photographs of a printed card work too; a person on our side checks those by hand.

PDF, JPG, PNG or HEIC. Up to 25 MB. Drag it here if you prefer.

If your menu already lives online. A link to a delivery-app listing does not work — we tested it and the data comes back wrong.

Where it lives

Your site needs an address. If you already own one we point it there; if you do not, it goes up on an address we give you the same day and you can move it to your own later without rebuilding anything.

Owning one means you pay for it somewhere: GoDaddy, Namecheap, Cloudflare, or whoever built your last site.

Then nothing else is needed here. You go live on an address like your-restaurant.netlify.app — real, secure, and yours to hand out from day one. When you buy a domain later, tell us and we move it across in an afternoon.

Just the name. No https://, no www.

Whoever you pay for it, or whoever set it up.

This is the question that matters most. Pointing a domain the wrong way is how a restaurant loses its email for two days — so we ask before we touch anything, not after.

Old site, booking page, landing pages, a shop — anything at that address today. If you can paste the current DNS records, even better; if that means nothing to you, describe it in words and we will find them.
